claim: In A. oryzae RIB40, hyphae on day 1 of cultivation contain 10–20 nuclei per cell.
source: In the model strain A. oryzae RIB40, hyphae on day 1 of cultivation contain 10–20 nuclei per cell, but by day 2 of cultivation, apical cells with more than 200 nuclei appear (Yasui et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yasui et al., 2020.

claim: By day 2 of cultivation, apical cells of A. oryzae RIB40 with more than 200 nuclei appear.
source: In the model strain A. oryzae RIB40, hyphae on day 1 of cultivation contain 10–20 nuclei per cell, but by day 2 of cultivation, apical cells with more than 200 nuclei appear (Yasui et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yasui et al., 2020.

claim: The proportion of hyphae with a higher number of nuclei (class III, over 200 nuclei in the cell) increased as the culture period increased from 1 to 3 days in A. oryzae RIB40.
source: We found that the proportion of hyphae with a higher number of nuclei (represented by class III, over 200 nuclei in the cell) increased as the culture period increased from 1 to 3 days (Figure 1A, B; Yasui et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, B and citation to Yasui et al., 2020.

claim: The phenotype of increased nuclear number was not observed in the model fungus Aspergillus nidulans.
source: This phenotype was not observed in the model fungus Aspergillus nidulans or the closely related species A. flavus (Figure 1A, B; Yasui et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, B and citation to Yasui et al., 2020.

claim: The phenotype of increased nuclear number was not observed in the closely related species A. flavus.
source: This phenotype was not observed in the model fungus Aspergillus nidulans or the closely related species A. flavus (Figure 1A, B; Yasui et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, B and citation to Yasui et al., 2020.

claim: The proportion of hyphae with a higher number of nuclei increased in Aspergillus sojae, which is used for miso and soy sauce production.
source: Among other Aspergillus species used in fermentation (Ichishima, 2016; Yamashita, 2021), the proportion of hyphae with a higher number of nuclei increased in Aspergillus sojae, which is used for miso and soy sauce production.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript and citations to Ichishima, 2016 and Yamashita, 2021.

claim: The phenotype of increased nuclear number was not observed in Aspergillus luchuensis.
source: This phenotype was not observed in Aspergillus luchuensis nor in its albino mutant Aspergillus luchuensis mut. kawachii, which are used for distilled spirits such as awamori and shochu.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: The phenotype of increased nuclear number was not observed in Aspergillus luchuensis mut. kawachii.
source: This phenotype was not observed in Aspergillus luchuensis nor in its albino mutant Aspergillus luchuensis mut. kawachii, which are used for distilled spirits such as awamori and shochu.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: The RIB915 strain of A. oryzae used for soy sauce fermentation does not show an increase in the number of nuclei.
source: Among several strains of A. oryzae used in industrial applications, the RIB915 strain used for soy sauce fermentation does not show an increase in the number of nuclei, while the RIB128 and RIB430 strains used in sake brewing exhibit a significant increase in the number of nuclei, suggesting that different phenotypes were selected through distinct breeding processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript and inference about breeding processes.

claim: The RIB128 and RIB430 strains of A. oryzae used in sake brewing exhibit a significant increase in the number of nuclei.
source: Among several strains of A. oryzae used in industrial applications, the RIB915 strain used for soy sauce fermentation does not show an increase in the number of nuclei, while the RIB128 and RIB430 strains used in sake brewing exhibit a significant increase in the number of nuclei, suggesting that different phenotypes were selected through distinct breeding processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript and inference about breeding processes.

claim: Different phenotypes of nuclear number increase were selected through distinct breeding processes in A. oryzae strains.
source: Among several strains of A. oryzae used in industrial applications, the RIB915 strain used for soy sauce fermentation does not show an increase in the number of nuclei, while the RIB128 and RIB430 strains used in sake brewing exhibit a significant increase in the number of nuclei, suggesting that different phenotypes were selected through distinct breeding processes.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on observed differences between strains.

claim: In class I hyphae of A. oryzae RIB40, nuclei are spaced relatively evenly.
source: In the class I hyphae, the nuclei were spaced relatively evenly, whereas in the class III hyphae with increased nuclei, the nuclei were densely packed and arranged in a disordered manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: In class III hyphae with increased nuclei, the nuclei are densely packed and arranged in a disordered manner.
source: In the class I hyphae, the nuclei were spaced relatively evenly, whereas in the class III hyphae with increased nuclei, the nuclei were densely packed and arranged in a disordered manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: The nuclear size in class III hyphae was significantly smaller than that in class I hyphae.
source: Furthermore, the nuclear size in the class III hyphae was significantly smaller than that in the class I hyphae (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: Nuclear division is synchronized in the hypha even when there are more than 200 nuclei.
source: Nuclear division is synchronized in the hypha even when there are more than 200 nuclei (Yasui et al., 2020), suggesting that DNA replication occurs similarly in most nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yasui et al., 2020.

claim: DNA replication occurs similarly in most nuclei in hyphae with more than 200 nuclei.
source: Nuclear division is synchronized in the hypha even when there are more than 200 nuclei (Yasui et al., 2020), suggesting that DNA replication occurs similarly in most nuclei.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of synchronized nuclear division.

claim: Nearly all nuclei in A. oryzae RIB40 possess normal genomes and chromosomes.
source: The germination rate of conidia and the colonies formed from individual conidia show no significant abnormalities, suggesting that nearly all nuclei possess normal genomes and chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations of normal germination and colony formation.

claim: Strains without an increase in nuclear number had hyphae with diameters ranging from 2 to 7 μm.
source: Strains without an increase in nuclear number had hyphae with diameters ranging from 2 to 7 μm, while strains with an increase in nuclear number had some hyphae of similar thickness but often exhibited thicker hyphae exceeding 10 μm (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Strains with an increase in nuclear number often exhibited thicker hyphae exceeding 10 μm.
source: Strains without an increase in nuclear number had hyphae with diameters ranging from 2 to 7 μm, while strains with an increase in nuclear number had some hyphae of similar thickness but often exhibited thicker hyphae exceeding 10 μm (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A strong positive correlation was observed between number of nuclei and cell volume in A. oryzae strains and A. flavus.
source: We compared the number of nuclei and cell volume within the first 100 μm from the hyphal tip, due to variation in the distance from the hyphal tip to the septum, among A. oryzae strains (RIB40, RIB128, and RIB915) and A. flavus (Figure 1G). A strong positive correlation was observed between number of nuclei and cell volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The number of nuclei per hyphal volume remains constant in filamentous fungi.
source: This is consistent with previously reported that the number of nuclei per hyphal volume remains constant (Dynesen and Nielsen, 2003; Dundon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dynesen and Nielsen, 2003 and Dundon et al., 2016.

claim: Thick hyphae with increased nuclei emerged by branching from hyphae without increased nuclei in A. oryzae RIB40.
source: Time-lapse imaging using the A. oryzae RIB40 expressing H2B-GFP indicated that thick hyphae with increased nuclei emerged by branching from hyphae without increased nuclei (Figure 2A, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Video 2.

claim: Rapid nuclear division occurred at the sites of branching in thick hyphae.
source: In the emerged thick hyphae, rapid nuclear division occurred at the sites of branching (Figure 2B, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Video 3.

claim: Immediately after branching, thick hyphae showed a significantly faster rate of nuclear proliferation, increasing four to five times within 8 hr compared to thin hyphae.
source: Immediately after branching, the thick hyphae showed a significantly faster rate of nuclear proliferation, increasing four to five times within 8 hr compared to the thin hyphae immediately after branching (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Branches from hyphae with increased nuclei produced both hyphae with and without increased nuclei.
source: Branches from hyphae with increased nuclei produced both hyphae with and without increased nuclei (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Thick hyphae elongated faster than thin hyphae in A. oryzae RIB40.
source: Since thick hyphae elongated faster than thin hyphae (Figure 2G), thick hyphae outgrew and overtook thin hyphae, eventually dominating the colony perimeter (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Thick hyphae outgrew and overtook thin hyphae, eventually dominating the colony perimeter.
source: Since thick hyphae elongated faster than thin hyphae (Figure 2G), thick hyphae outgrew and overtook thin hyphae, eventually dominating the colony perimeter (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E, F and inferred from the faster elongation rate.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed basic nuclear structures, such as the nuclear membrane and nucleolus, in both thick and thin hyphae.
source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed basic nuclear structures, such as the nuclear membrane and nucleolus, in both thick and thin hyphae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: As hyphal diameter increased, cell walls became more uneven and thicker.
source: As hyphal diameter increased, cell walls became more uneven and thicker (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2H, I.

claim: Raman spectroscopy results showed pronounced peaks corresponding to cell wall polysaccharides in thick hyphae.
source: This finding corresponds with Raman spectroscopy results showing pronounced peaks corresponding to cell wall polysaccharides in thick hyphae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Hossain et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by Raman spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citation to Hossain et al., 2023.

claim: Peaks associated with active mitochondria were prominent in thick hyphae.
source: Additionally, peaks associated with active mitochondria were prominent in thick hyphae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Yasuda et al., 2019), which was further confirmed by fluorescence staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Raman spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, fluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, and citation to Yasuda et al., 2019.

claim: Thick hyphae exhibited greater surface roughness compared to thin hyphae.
source: Thick hyphae exhibited greater surface roughness and higher elasticity compared to thin hyphae (Figure 2J, K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 2J, K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Thick hyphae exhibited higher elasticity compared to thin hyphae.
source: Thick hyphae exhibited greater surface roughness and higher elasticity compared to thin hyphae (Figure 2J, K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 2J, K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Strains that show an increase in nuclear number had significantly higher levels of protein secretion than strains that do not.
source: We compared the amounts of secreted proteins in A. oryzae RIB40, RIB128, RIB915, A. nidulans, and A. flavus (Figure 3A). The strains that show an increase in nuclear number had significantly higher levels of protein secretion than the strains that do not.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: α-amylases are the dominant proteins secreted by A. oryzae under the tested condition.
source: In this condition, α-amylases are the dominant proteins secreted by A. oryzae (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: In A. oryzae RIB40, starting from day 2, when hyphae with increased nuclear numbers appeared, the enzyme activity per fungal biomass significantly increased more than RIB915.
source: In RIB40, starting from day 2, when hyphae with increased nuclear numbers appeared, the enzyme activity per fungal biomass significantly increased more than RIB915 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After 12 hr, the fluorescence intensity in the channel with thick hyphae was about three times higher than that in the channel with thin hyphae, indicating that thicker hyphae secreted more amylase than thinner hyphae.
source: After 12 hr, the fluorescence intensity in the channel with thick hyphae was about three times higher than that in the channel with thin hyphae, indicating that thicker hyphae secreted more amylase than thinner hyphae (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D from microfluidic device experiments.

claim: The addition of yeast extract increased both hyphal width and nuclear number in the RIB915 strain.
source: We found that the addition of yeast extract increased both hyphal width and nuclear number in the RIB915 strain (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In A. oryzae RIB40, the addition of yeast extract did not make the already thick hyphae any thicker but increased the proportion of thicker hyphae.
source: In A. oryzae RIB40, the addition of yeast extract did not make the already thick hyphae any thicker but increased the proportion of thicker hyphae.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of yeast extract increased protein secretion approximately 1.8 times in RIB40 and 8.5 times in RIB915.
source: The addition of yeast extract increased protein secretion approximately 1.8 times in RIB40 and 8.5 times in RIB915 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The addition of yeast extract to A. nidulans increased hyphal width by 1.4 times and protein secretion by 5.1 times.
source: Although the addition of yeast extract did not cause a dramatic increase in nuclear number in A. nidulans, hyphal width increased by 1.4 times and protein secretion increased by 5.1 times.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of nucleic acids, peptone, or casamino acids to the minimal medium increased the number of nuclei in A. oryzae RIB915.
source: The addition of nucleic acids, peptone, or casamino acids to the minimal medium increased the number of nuclei in A. oryzae RIB915, while vitamin B did not cause a significant change in nuclear number (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Vitamin B did not cause a significant change in nuclear number in A. oryzae RIB915.
source: The addition of nucleic acids, peptone, or casamino acids to the minimal medium increased the number of nuclei in A. oryzae RIB915, while vitamin B did not cause a significant change in nuclear number (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The addition of asparagine, proline, glutamine, and branched-chain amino acids increased the proportion of hyphae with increased nuclei by 40–50% in A. oryzae RIB915.
source: Although the addition of individual amino acids did not show the same effect as yeast extract, the addition of asparagine, proline, glutamine, and branched-chain amino acids increased the proportion of hyphae with increased nuclei by 40–50% (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The amino acids that induced nuclear number increase also led to an increase in protein secretion.
source: The amino acids that induced nuclear number increase also led to an increase in protein secretion, indicating a positive correlation between the ratio of class III hyphae and the increase in secreted proteins (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the ratio of class III hyphae and the increase in secreted proteins.
source: The amino acids that induced nuclear number increase also led to an increase in protein secretion, indicating a positive correlation between the ratio of class III hyphae and the increase in secreted proteins (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A. oryzae RIB40 grown with low concentration of rapamycin did not produce hyphae with an increased number of nuclei.
source: Since the amino acids inducing an increase in nuclear number may activate the Target of Rapamycin (TOR) pathway (Wouters and Koritzinsky, 2008), A. oryzae RIB40 was grown with low concentration of rapamycin, a TOR pathway inhibitor, which minimally affects colony size. Under the conditions, RIB40 did not produce hyphae with an increased number of nuclei (Figure 3I–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3I–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and citation to Wouters and Koritzinsky, 2008.

claim: Rapamycin decreased the ratio of hyphae with increased nuclei even in the medium with yeast extract.
source: Rapamycin decreased the ratio of hyphae with increased nuclei even in the medium with yeast extract (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In RIB915, supplementation with yeast extract led to a more than fourfold increase in the expression of 660 genes.
source: In RIB915, supplementation with yeast extract led to a more than fourfold increase in the expression of 660 genes, among which 449 genes did not show such increase in RIB40 or A. nidulans (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 449 genes upregulated in RIB915 with yeast extract did not show such increase in RIB40 or A. nidulans.
source: In RIB915, supplementation with yeast extract led to a more than fourfold increase in the expression of 660 genes, among which 449 genes did not show such increase in RIB40 or A. nidulans (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Gene ontology analysis of 449 genes uniquely upregulated in RIB915 with yeast extract revealed that processes related to cell wall synthesis and divalent metal ion transport were significantly enriched.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of these genes revealed that processes related to cell wall synthesis and divalent metal ion transport were significantly enriched (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Clear differences in gene expression pattern were observed between thick and thin hyphae in A. oryzae RIB40.
source: To capture gene expression changes associated with increased nuclei with higher resolution, thick and thin hyphae from RIB40 were dissected using laser microdissection, collected separately, and subjected to transcriptome analysis (Figure 4D, Video 6). Clear differences in gene expression pattern were observed between thick and thin hyphae (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 558 genes were more than fourfold upregulated in thick hyphae but not in thin hyphae.
source: 558 genes that were more than fourfold upregulated in thick hyphae but not in thin hyphae (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: GO analysis of genes upregulated in thick hyphae indicated an enrichment of processes related to biogenesis of ribosome and cellular component.
source: GO analysis of the upregulated genes indicated an enrichment of processes related to biogenesis of ribosome and cellular component (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 21 genes matched between those upregulated in RIB915 with yeast extract and those upregulated in thick hyphae of RIB40.
source: Among them, 21 matched those from (Figure 4G, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Of the 21 matched genes, 13 had GO annotations related to conidiation, cell wall synthesis, Ca2+ transport, and rRNA processing.
source: Of these, 13 had GO annotations, which were related to conidiation, cell wall synthesis, Ca2+ transport, and rRNA processing (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Overall ribosomal gene expression increased in the thick hyphae than the thin hyphae.
source: KEGG map visualization indicates that overall ribosomal gene expression increased in the thick hyphae than the thin hyphae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Disruption of msyA in A. oryzae RIB40 did not have a significant impact on colony growth, hyphal morphology, and number of nuclei in minimal medium.
source: Disruption of the ortholog genes, msyA and msyB, in A. oryzae RIB40 did not have a significant impact on colony growth, hyphal morphology, and number of nuclei in minimal medium (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Under hypoosmotic shock conditions, the △msyA often indicated cell lysis near the hyphal tips.
source: Under hypoosmotic shock conditions, the △msyA often indicated cell lysis near the hyphal tips (Figure 4I, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4I, J.

claim: The msyA disruption impairs the regulation of the hyphal cell expansion, leading to hyphal lysis under hypoosmotic conditions.
source: Under hypoosmotic conditions, water influx into the cells causes hyphal cell expansion, but the volume and turgor pressure are regulated to prevent cell lysis. The msyA disruption, however, impairs the regulation of the hyphal cell expansion, leading to hyphal lysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E and inference from the observed phenotype.

claim: In the minimal media supplemented with yeast extract, all 20 A. oryzae strains from six different clades exhibited an increase in nuclear number.
source: We investigated whether nuclear numbers increase in 20 strains selected from six different clades (Figure 5A). In the minimal media supplemented with yeast extract, all strains exhibited an increase in nuclear number (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the minimal media without yeast extract, three strains from Clade C showed an increase in nuclear number.
source: In the minimal media without yeast extract, three strains from Clade C showed an increase in nuclear number, whereas strains from Clades A, B, and E did not (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Strains from Clades A, B, and E did not show an increase in nuclear number in minimal media without yeast extract.
source: In the minimal media without yeast extract, three strains from Clade C showed an increase in nuclear number, whereas strains from Clades A, B, and E did not (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Clades F and G included both strains with increased nuclear numbers and strains without.
source: Clades F and G included both strains with increased nuclear numbers and strains without.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: SNP analysis of ORFs in clade F revealed 108 mutations between TK-32 and TK-38.
source: SNP analysis of ORFs in clades F and G revealed 108 mutations in clade F between TK-32 and TK-38, and 23 mutations in clade G between TK-41 and TK-47 (Supplementary file 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by SNP analysis data in Supplementary file 4 and 5.

claim: SNP analysis of ORFs in clade G revealed 23 mutations between TK-41 and TK-47.
source: SNP analysis of ORFs in clades F and G revealed 108 mutations in clade F between TK-32 and TK-38, and 23 mutations in clade G between TK-41 and TK-47 (Supplementary file 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by SNP analysis data in Supplementary file 4 and 5.

claim: rseA (AO090038000626), a predicted glycosyl transferase, was the only common gene among mutations in clades F and G.
source: Among these, AO090038000626; rseA, predicted glycosyl transferase, was the only common gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by SNP analysis data.

claim: rseA has been identified as a mutation in an A. sojae mutant with high extracellular enzyme production.
source: This gene has been identified as a mutation in an A. sojae mutant with high extracellular enzyme production (Ogawa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ogawa et al., 2021.

claim: Deletion of rseA in A. nidulans leads to cell wall defects and promotes enzyme secretion.
source: It is also shown that deletion of rseA in A. nidulans leads to cell wall defects and promotes enzyme secretion (Ogawa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ogawa et al., 2021.

claim: Comparison of mutations in rseA among strains in clades C, F, and G indicates a few amino acid substitutions within the ORF, but no common mutations corresponded to the phenotype.
source: Comparison of mutations in rseA among strains in clades C, F, and G indicates a few amino acid substitutions within the ORF, but no common mutations corresponded to the phenotype (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Structural prediction suggests that the mutations in rseA are located inside the enzyme domain.
source: Structural prediction suggests that the mutations are located inside the enzyme domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural prediction data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The disruption of rseA in A. oryzae RIB40 resulted in significant growth delay, increased branching, and the absence of hyphae with increased nuclei.
source: The disruption of the rseA in A. oryzae RIB40 resulted in significant growth delay, increased branching, and the absence of hyphae with increased nuclei (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: RIB915 strains expressing rseA from RIB40 or TK-47 exhibited an increase in hyphal width and a corresponding increase in the proportion of hyphae with more nuclei.
source: The strains expressing rseA from RIB40 or TK-47 exhibited an increase in hyphal width and a corresponding increase in the proportion of hyphae with more nuclei, whereas the strain expressing rseA from TK41 showed no increase in hyphal width or nuclear number (Figure 5E, F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RIB915 strain expressing rseA from TK41 showed no increase in hyphal width or nuclear number.
source: The strains expressing rseA from RIB40 or TK-47 exhibited an increase in hyphal width and a corresponding increase in the proportion of hyphae with more nuclei, whereas the strain expressing rseA from TK41 showed no increase in hyphal width or nuclear number (Figure 5E, F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In minimal medium, no significant differences in hyphal width or nuclear number were observed between the bred and control strains of T. reesei and P. chrysogenum.
source: In minimal medium, no significant differences in hyphal width or nuclear number were observed between the bred and control strains, whereas with the addition of yeast extract, a notable increase in nuclear number and hyphal width was observed only in the bred strains (Figure 5G, H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G, H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: With the addition of yeast extract, a notable increase in nuclear number and hyphal width was observed only in the bred strains of T. reesei and P. chrysogenum.
source: In minimal medium, no significant differences in hyphal width or nuclear number were observed between the bred and control strains, whereas with the addition of yeast extract, a notable increase in nuclear number and hyphal width was observed only in the bred strains (Figure 5G, H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G, H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The addition of yeast extract significantly increased cellulase activity only in the bred strain of T. reesei.
source: The addition of yeast extract significantly increased cellulase and protease activity only in the bred strain of T. reesei and P. chrysogenum, respectively (Figure 5I, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The addition of yeast extract significantly increased protease activity only in the bred strain of P. chrysogenum.
source: The addition of yeast extract significantly increased cellulase and protease activity only in the bred strain of T. reesei and P. chrysogenum, respectively (Figure 5I, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Even in modern biotechnology, where high enzyme or compound producing strains are bred, strains with increased nuclear numbers were selected, like the traditional breeding practices of koji-fungi.
source: These results suggest that even in modern biotechnology, where high enzyme or compound producing strains are bred, strains with increased nuclear numbers were selected, like the traditional breeding practices of koji-fungi.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that bred strains of T. reesei and P. chrysogenum show increased nuclear numbers.

claim: In A. oryzae some strains, hyphae grow about three times thicker and contain roughly ten times more nuclei than the initial hyphae.
source: In A. oryzae some strains, hyphae grow about three times thicker and contain roughly ten times more nuclei than the initial hyphae (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio is tightly regulated in organisms from unicellular yeast to multicellular plants and animals.
source: This consistency aligns with findings in other organisms, from unicellular yeast to multicellular plants and animals, where the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio is tightly regulated, allowing cell cycle progression only upon reaching a critical cell size (Amodeo and Skotheim, 2016; Nurse, 1975; Jorgensen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amodeo and Skotheim, 2016; Nurse, 1975; Jorgensen et al., 2007.

claim: Cell cycle progression is allowed only upon reaching a critical cell size.
source: This consistency aligns with findings in other organisms, from unicellular yeast to multicellular plants and animals, where the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio is tightly regulated, allowing cell cycle progression only upon reaching a critical cell size (Amodeo and Skotheim, 2016; Nurse, 1975; Jorgensen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amodeo and Skotheim, 2016; Nurse, 1975; Jorgensen et al., 2007.
